claims.text: The initial eutectic high-entropy alloy has a uniform microstructure.
Controlled thermomechanical processing can create a hierarchical or composite microstructure in eutectic high-entropy alloys.
The proposed processing intervention will produce a bimodal grain-size distribution.
A bimodal hierarchical microstructure will increase strength under ambient-temperature uniaxial tensile loading.
A bimodal hierarchical microstructure will increase ductility under ambient-temperature uniaxial tensile loading.
Strength will increase by 15% relative to a conventional uniform-microstructure eutectic high-entropy alloy.
Ductility will increase by 20% relative to a conventional uniform-microstructure eutectic high-entropy alloy.
The hierarchical microstructure introduces additional grain boundaries.
The additional grain boundaries impede dislocation motion.
Impeded dislocation motion increases alloy strength.
The larger-grain population provides sufficient strain-hardening capacity.
Strain-hardening capacity supplied by the larger grains maintains ductility.
The magnitude of improvement may depend on alloy composition, processing conditions, and testing methodology.
The bimodal grain-size distribution may not be achieved uniformly throughout the material.
Nonuniform realization of the bimodal grain-size distribution may affect the overall property enhancement.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis predicts 15% higher strength and 20% higher ductility, but the falsification rule only rejects results below 10% and 15%, respectively. Results between these values would fail the stated quantitative prediction without falsifying it under the proposed rule.
